note: Target vanishing-point article, coreSummary and section “A detailed account written decades later,” says the fullest surviving account is Manetti's Life of Brunelleschi, dated by scholars to the 1480s, while the panels are proposed as c.1401–1425; it says manuscript attribution is unsettled. This supports the bridge's qualified point that the account was written decades after the demonstration and attribution is not fully settled.
sentence: An ancient technique's founding account can stay just as thin elsewhere in art history: [the fullest surviving description of Brunelleschi's vanishing-point demonstration panels was written decades after the fact, by a biographer whose own authorship of that account isn't fully settled either](/vanishing-point/).

note: Target elements-of-art article, coreSummary and section “Seven terms, one textbook,” identifies the 1968 printing of Ocvirk's Art Fundamentals as one documented setting for the seven-item list, while explicitly saying it does not establish the list's first appearance. This supports the bridge's narrow statement that a 1968 printing documents the list, not an ancient origin.
sentence: The seven-part vocabulary now used to describe any painting's structure, line, shape, form, has a similarly recent history: [a 1968 printing of a studio-art textbook documents the seven-item list](/elements-of-art/), which is a long way from any inherited ancient tradition, however timeless the terms sound.
